newsitem.title: JAPAN: New British trade chief promises EMU decisiveness.
newsitem.headline: New British trade chief promises EMU decisiveness.

text.p: Britain's new trade chief Margaret Beckett promised Japanese business on Tuesday the new Labour government would be decisive and hard-headed when the time came to decide on whether to join a single European currency.
Without hinting at Labour's decision on European economic and monetary union (EMU), or when it would be taken, Beckett said there would be no hesitation once the choice was made.

Making her first foreign trip since Labour won power three weeks ago, Beckett said she was surprised to learn how important the issue was to Japanese businesses as they decide where to invest in Europe in the coming years.

"I have been slightly surprised that there was so much more focus on the single currency than there was on some of the other issues that tend to be raised domestically in Britain," Beckett told Reuters in an interview.
"But they would rather we got the decision right than we made it fast," she added.

Beckett, the secretary of trade and industry, spent much of the second day of a three-day visit fielding questions from Japanese businessmen and the media about British intentions in Europe now that Labour was in power.
Britain is Japan's biggest manufacturing base in Europe, but the single currency question has thrown a cloud over whether this will continue into the 21st century.
There are at present 259 Japanese companies with plants in Britain, representing nearly 40 percent of total Japanese manufacturing investment in the EU.
Media reports in recent weeks have mentioned France, Spain, Germany, Poland and Slovakia as possible sites for Japanese car plants that Britain might once have regarded as their own.
Beckett's reply each time Europe was raised was the same: the new Labour government was fully committed again to Europe and wanted to take part in decisions about the region's future.

Beckett assured the Japanese they should not fear labour strife under the new government or worry that Labour's plans to engage fully again with Europe would mean rising costs, a key reason for Japanese plants initially setting up in Britain.

"There will be no blanket repeal of the (British) 1980's employment and trade union laws on ballots and strikes," she said in a speech on the royal yacht Britannia to a group of top Japanese businessmen.
The yacht, making a stopover on its way to the Hong Kong handover ceremonies at the end of June, was the site of several trade-related functions during Beckett's visit.
"Signing up to the (EU) social charter also does not mean importing wholesale the social security or labour market systems of other European countries," she added.
But she stood firm in vowing that Labour would bring in a minimum wage, saying it was a scandal that Britain alone of developed countries did not give protection to low paid workers.
Beckett chose her words more carefully on the vexed question of a single currency, but said there would not be what she called the "drift" of the previous Conservative government.
"The decision will be decided on the basis of a hard-headed assessment of Britain's national interests. So I'm afraid I'm not going to set a date today," she said.
"But if Britain's interests say go in, then this British government will take Britain in," she said in a speech to the British Chamber of Commerce in Tokyo.
